Port Ellery, Halloween night,
1936. Opening night of THE
RAVEN'S BRIDE at the Paragon
Theatre. In Act III the heroine
stabs the villain with a trick
dagger, and the villain -
Victor Crane, the Paragon's
owner and star - falls down
dead. The dagger was real.

You are Inspector Ada Penn of
Homicide, and you have until
dawn. Search the empty theater
with the house lights up, then
again at 2 AM with only the
ghost light burning. Question
the leading lady, the
understudy, the widow, the
stage manager and the critic.
Then gather them on the stage
and name the killer - and say
how, and why.

pages.head: The Case
pages.html:
Final Curtain

An Inspector Ada Penn Mystery

Port Ellery, Saturday, October 31, 1936.

Opening night at the Paragon Theatre. The house is sold out for THE RAVEN'S BRIDE, a new melodrama written by, directed by and starring the Paragon's owner, Victor Crane.

In Act III, the bride Rowena (the lovely Lila Fontaine) stabs the wicked Count Corvin with a trick dagger, the kind whose blade slides into the handle. Victor Crane falls, as he has at every rehearsal. Six hundred people applaud.

He does not get up for his curtain call.

The dagger in his heart is real: an antique blade with a raven's head on the pommel. The audience has been sent home, the cast and crew are held in the green room, and the rain has not stopped. At half past ten a police car pulls up under the marquee, and Inspector Ada Penn of Homicide steps out.

She has until dawn.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type FINAL and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster (or compatible) plays the music and the digitized sounds; without one, the PC speaker does its best.

The Paragon appears in the rain. Press a key for the menu, then pick Play. Read Storyline shows the death scene again, and Read Instructions has the keys. Leave the menu alone for half a minute and Ada will show you around the box office and the wings herself.

Sergeant Dobbs meets you at the stage door and asks whose card the print on the trick dagger matches. The lab's fingerprint sheet in the box has the answer, if you look through the spyglass; step on a name to say. A wrong name costs nothing and neither does skipping it: walk to the door marked GO IN. The print only shows who held the prop, never who swapped it.

The case is told in five parts, and the card at the start of each one says which part you are in (PART 1 OF 5, and so on):

  • Act One, 10:30 PM. Search the empty theater with the house lights up.
  • The Green Room. Question the five suspects.
  • Act Two, 2:00 AM. Search again by the ghost light, with Mrs. Crane's keys.
  • The Green Room, 2 AM. Question them again and show them what you found.
  • Dawn. Name the killer on the stage.

F5 saves a case and F6 loads one. Save at the start of each part, and always before you accuse anyone!

pages.head: Controls
pages.html:
Controls

KeyWhat it does
Arrows or W A S DWalk
Q / EWalk up and to the left / up and to the right
Number pad 7 9 1 3Walk on the four diagonals
SpacePick up what you are standing on
ZLook through the lens (once you carry it)
F1Help
F2What you carry, your score, evidence and chances
F3 / F4Music / sound on and off
F5 / F6Save / load a case
EscGive up and go back to the menu

A joystick walks in all eight directions; its first button picks things up.

F2 is the status page: it counts your evidence and your chances.

pages.head: Searching the Paragon
pages.html:
Searching the Paragon

Evidence lies where it fell. Stand on it and press Space. Each piece rings a little chord and adds one to your evidence count.

Read the walls. Not everything can be carried. Notes pinned up and chalked on boards tell their own story: the bar's tab board, the box office count, the letter tucked in a dressing-room mirror, the playbill in Victor's office, the Historical Society's clippings in the lobby. Write down what they say.

Keys. Some doors are locked. A key goes on your ring when you walk over it, and is used up by the door it opens.

The green room door counts your evidence. Push it once and it takes your notes to look them over; push again and it gives them back and swings open. If you haven't found enough, it stays shut.

pages.head: Tools of the Trade
pages.html:
Tools of the Trade

The magnifying glass

The Paragon staged a Sherlock Holmes play two seasons ago, and the props room still has his glass. Carry it, and small things that nobody else would notice show up when you walk over them. Press Z to look through it.

It reads bad print, too. Push against a smudged word and the glass sets it right, one letter at a time.

The lantern

At 2 AM the power is off. Under the stage it is black as pitch: the floor and the walls only show where your lantern has been, one flagstone at a time. Listen for your footsteps, feel along the walls, and watch for red eyes.

Victor's safe

Three dials and a door. Push against a dial to turn it to the next symbol: a mask, a raven, a rose, a moon. Victor was a vain man who never wrote anything down that he could hang on a wall instead.

pages.head: Questioning
pages.html:
Questioning

In the green room, walk up to a suspect to sit down across the table from them. The floor holds question cards. Step on a card to ask that question; when they have answered, you are back in your chair to ask another. The EXIT card ends the talk.

The second time round, after Act Two, the cards carry the evidence you found: SHOW it to them and watch their faces.

The evidence board on the green room wall holds your notes on every piece you have found, and the coroner's report. Step up to a card to read it again.

People lie. Paper doesn't. When a witness and a piece of evidence disagree, believe the evidence.

pages.head: Who's Who
pages.html:
Who's Who

Name
Victor CraneOwner and star of the Paragon. Count Corvin. The victim.
Lila FontaineLeading lady: the Raven's Bride. She struck the blow.
Edgar BlissVictor's understudy. Played the Herald in Act I, then had the night off.
Agatha CraneVictor's wife, now his widow, and co-owner. Keeps the books.
Felix MorrowStage manager and prop master, thirty years at the Paragon.
Oliver PikeDrama critic of the Port Ellery Courier, in a complimentary seat.
Sgt. Walter DobbsYour sergeant. Holds doors. Makes coffee.
Commissioner HaleYour boss. Will not wait for a fourth guess.
MacbethThe theater cat. Not a suspect.

Things that go bump at 2 AM: the night watchman on his rounds (he won't let you past), the wisps from the ghost light (they cost you points), and the rats under the stage.

pages.head: Naming the Killer
pages.html:
Naming the Killer

At dawn the suspects stand in a row on the stage. Step into the spotlight in front of the one you accuse. If you are not ready, the BACK OFF card returns you to the green room.

Name the right one and they will ask you HOW it was done, and then WHY. Each is a choice of three cards. You need all three answers.

A wrong answer brings Commissioner Hale, who explains exactly why you are wrong, and gives you a strike. You have three chances: the third strike takes you off the case.

Scoring

  • Evidence: 100 points a piece; the hidden pieces are worth more
  • Opening the safe: 200
  • Reading the plaque in the lobby: 1,776
  • Solving the case: 5,000
  • A wrong answer: -500
  • Every scare costs a few points

items.title: The Port Ellery Courier
items.headline: STAR SLAIN ON STAGE
items.deck: Victor Crane falls in Act III of his own play; the dagger was real. Police hold cast at the Paragon.
columns:
PORT ELLERY, Oct. 31. - Six hundred playgoers at the Paragon Theatre tonight applauded what they believed was the finest death scene of the season, only to learn that Victor Crane, 52, the theater's owner and the star of its new melodrama, THE RAVEN'S BRIDE, was in fact dead.

Mr. Crane, as the villainous Count Corvin, was struck at 9:48 by the heroine Rowena, played by Miss Lila Fontaine, with what should have been a harmless stage dagger.

Police say the weapon was a genuine antique blade. Inspector Ada Penn of Homicide arrived shortly after ten and ordered the company held in the theater's green room.

Mrs. Agatha Crane, the widow and co-owner, declined to comment. The play's second performance has been canceled. Mr. Edgar Bliss, Mr. Crane's understudy, is expected to assume the role when the house reopens.

OUR CRITIC'S VIEW. The Courier's drama critic, Mr. Oliver Pike, was in attendance. His review, filed before the tragedy was known, will not be printed. Of the play itself Mr. Pike remarked only that it was "rather good. Surprisingly good, for Victor."

photo.caption: The stage of the Paragon after the house was cleared. Police photograph.

briefs: The weather bureau promises rain through Tuesday.
Theater custom keeps one bulb lit on an empty stage all night.
Tag no. 13, Paragon cloakroom. Owner may claim it at Police HQ.
The Historical Society's archives committee has hung its July 1776 plaque and old Courier clippings at the Paragon.
A 1931 item in these pages printed a new play's title as "Rayen Brine." The Courier regrets the error, five years late.
Remington Noiseless typewriter. Types without a sound, which some find unnerving. $75. Box 1936.

items.title: Final Curtain Hint Book
items.note: Read the answers through the red film
items.intro: Stuck on a case? Lay the red film over an answer to read it. Read only the hint you need: the fun is in the deducing.

hints.q: Sergeant Dobbs asks whose card the dagger's print matches.
hints.a: Lila Fontaine's, the first name. The lab sheet's lifted print is her round whorl, turned and smudged. A wrong card costs nothing, and the GO IN door is open either way.

hints.q: Where do I start?
hints.a: The box office, off the west side of the lobby. There is a key on the floor and the seating chart on the desk.

hints.q: How do I get backstage from the house?
hints.a: Take the west aisle to the front, then go up through the pass door in the corner at stage left.

hints.q: Victor's office is locked.
hints.a: The key from the box office opens it. Walk into the door.

hints.q: I have three pieces of evidence and can't find a fourth.
hints.a: Get the magnifying glass from the props room shelves, then walk the floor in front of the prop table in the stage-right wing.

hints.q: The green room door won't open.
hints.a: It needs all four pieces of Act One evidence: the seating chart, the checklist, the ticket stub and the insurance policy. Push it, then push again.

hints.q: It's too dark under the stage.
hints.a: Get the night watchman's lantern from the WATCH room at the east end of the corridor. Everywhere you walk lights up.

hints.q: How do I get under the stage?
hints.a: Through the pit gate on the east side of the front rail, along the orchestra pit, and through the PIT door.

hints.q: What is the safe's combination?
hints.a: The playbill on the office wall: RAVEN, ROSE, MOON, left to right. Push each dial until it shows its symbol.

hints.q: Where is the fourth piece in Act Two?
hints.a: Beyond the trap room maze: a doorway in its far south-east corner, open only tonight, leads into the old prop vault. The rats are harmless, but they cost you points.

hints.q: The watchman keeps getting in my way.
hints.a: He only walks the south half of the corridor. Keep to the north side.

hints.q: Who has an alibi?
hints.a: Lila (Mrs. Hobbs), Edgar (the bar tab chalked at 9:05 and 9:15), Agatha (the box office count signed 9:10) and Felix (his crew). One suspect has nobody to vouch for him.

hints.q: Who lied?
hints.a: The critic. He says he never left seat F-9, but his stub was under the prop table and his umbrella left the cloakroom at 9:05.

hints.q: What does the clipping in the lobby say?
hints.a: It's a misprint. Carry the lens and push against each smudged word: PIKE'S PLAY: RAVEN BRIDE, back in 1931.

hints.q: Is the plaque worth reading?
hints.a: Exactly 1,776 points' worth. Push against its middle.

hints.q: Who did it?
hints.a: Oliver Pike, the critic.

hints.q: How?
hints.a: He swapped the trick dagger for a real one at the prop table during the interval. There was no poison, and the Act III blackout had been cut.

hints.q: Why?
hints.a: Victor Crane stole his play. Pike wrote THE RAVEN'S BRIDE in 1931; the manuscript was in Victor's safe.

hints.q: Some say the felt-maker left something behind in the theater.
hints.a: Somewhere comfy, and only after midnight. Bring your magnifying glass.

hints.q: Where, after midnight?
hints.a: The green room, at 2 AM. The sofa looks like any sofa, until you look closer.

hints.q: I give up. Spell it out.
hints.a: At 2 AM, carry the magnifying glass from the props room into the green room. Stand just left of the sofa in the bottom right corner and push right into it (it costs one lens charge). The egg shows between the cushions: push again to take it, then step into the empty seat.

items.title: A note found in the green room
items.body:
You will remember the play. You laughed at it in this very office five years ago. Tonight six hundred people will see it with your name on the program.

Enjoy your death scene.

news.head: Final Curtain: our first whodunit
news.html: Port Ellery, Halloween night, 1936. Six hundred people watched Victor Crane die in Act III of THE RAVEN'S BRIDE and thought it was acting. In Final Curtain you are Inspector Ada Penn of Homicide, and you have until dawn. Search the Paragon with the house lights up, then again by the ghost light; question five suspects, then show them what you found. Name the killer, how and why. Commissioner Hale gives you three chances.

news.head: Since last issue: The Big Show went on
news.html: Teddy's Little Big Adventure is the most-played game on our BBS this summer. Play dead is still the favorite trick (it's the only way past the Pie-O-Matic), and the most-asked question is how high a corgi can hop. Two blocks easily, three with good steering, four never. A wall that tall always has another way around.

news.head: Around the Sandbox: Trick or treat
news.html: On Halloween night Doc Leo will be at the office door with balloon animals for the trick-or-treaters: dogs, swords and, by special request, one very long giraffe. Teddy is going as a knight again. Gwinn is going as Gwinn; she ate the other costume. THE CHEZ is going as a pumpkin, which, being tomato red, it already mostly is.

news.head: In the workshop: A library in a box
news.html: Remember the Dog House, the tiny red lending library on a post on Maple Street in Teddy's adventure? We looked inside. It's much bigger than the box. KEEP IT BRIEF! is about the night every word fell out of every book, and the tin night librarian who has to put them back, exactly one hundred words at a time.

news.head: Letters: "Is the Clown Club real?"
news.html:
"Teddy, Gwinn, Doc Leo, the Big Show... is the Clown Club real?" - A reader, age 9

The Scoop replies: Very real. Doc Leo marches in its parades, and the Clown Club puts on shows for kids all over town. In real life there are fewer custard pies.
